claim: Mechanosensory feedback enhances the recruitment of motor pools during active locomotion in zebrafish larvae.
source: We show that mechanosensory feedback enhances the recruitment of motor pools during active locomotion.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data comparing active and fictive locomotion.

claim: Inputs from mechanosensory neurons increase locomotor speed by prolonging fast swimming at the expense of slow swimming during stereotyped acoustic escape responses.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that inputs from mechanosensory neurons increase locomotor speed by prolonging fast swimming at the expense of slow swimming during stereotyped acoustic escape responses.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by kinematic analysis data presented in the results.

claim: Connections compatible with monosynaptic inputs from mechanosensory Rohon-Beard neurons onto ipsilateral V2a interneurons selectively recruited at high speed can contribute to the observed enhancement of speed.
source: In the spinal cord, we show that connections compatible with monosynaptic inputs from mechanosensory Rohon-Beard neurons onto ipsilateral V2a interneurons selectively recruited at high speed can contribute to the observed enhancement of speed.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by optogenetic circuit mapping experiments.

claim: Premotor excitatory V2a interneurons and motor neurons are recruited in a frequency-dependent manner.
source: At the level of locomotor circuits in the spinal cord, premotor excitatory V2a interneurons and motor neurons are recruited in a frequency-dependent manner (Crone et al., 2008; Kimura et al., 2006; McLean et al., 2007), a feature thought to underlie speed control in zebrafish (McLean et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Distinct microcircuit modules could regulate the mobilization of individual muscles during locomotion.
source: Recently, circuit-mapping experiments revealed preferential connectivity profiles between identified groups of V2a interneurons and motor neurons suggesting that distinct microcircuit modules could regulate the mobilization of individual muscles during locomotion (Ampatzis et al., 2014; Bagnall and McLean, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous circuit-mapping studies.

claim: Genetic ablation of V2a interneurons in mammals is associated with deficits in left-right coordination and gait transitions.
source: Genetic ablation of V2a interneurons in mammals is associated with deficits in left-right coordination and gait transitions suggesting that V2a interneurons play a key role in controlling speed across vertebrates (Crone et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: V2a interneurons play a key role in controlling speed across vertebrates.
source: Genetic ablation of V2a interneurons in mammals is associated with deficits in left-right coordination and gait transitions suggesting that V2a interneurons play a key role in controlling speed across vertebrates (Crone et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cited ablation study results.

claim: Peripheral mechanosensory feedback plays a critical role in setting the timing of muscle activation during movement.
source: Peripheral mechanosensory feedback plays a critical role in setting the timing of muscle activation during movement (Windhorst, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Stimulation of afferent sensory neurons in decerebrate and paralyzed cats can reorganize the pattern of motor output during fictive locomotion.
source: In particular, stimulation of afferent sensory neurons in decerebrate and paralyzed cats can reorganize the pattern of motor output during fictive locomotion, either by entraining or resetting the locomotor rhythm, depending on the nature of active spinal circuits (Conway et al., 1987; Guertin et al., 1995; Jankowska, 1992; McCrea, 2001; Rossignol et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Altering the development of peripheral sensory neurons leads to dramatic perturbations of motor sequences during walking and swimming in mice.
source: In addition, altering the development of peripheral sensory neurons leads to dramatic perturbations of motor sequences during walking and swimming in mice, suggesting that mechanosensory circuits can directly control the activity of spinal central pattern generators responsible for rhythmic motor outputs (Akay et al., 2014; Takeoka et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mechanosensory circuits can directly control the activity of spinal central pattern generators responsible for rhythmic motor outputs.
source: In addition, altering the development of peripheral sensory neurons leads to dramatic perturbations of motor sequences during walking and swimming in mice, suggesting that mechanosensory circuits can directly control the activity of spinal central pattern generators responsible for rhythmic motor outputs (Akay et al., 2014; Takeoka et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cited studies on sensory neuron perturbations.

claim: GFP-Aequorin was expressed selectively in spinal motor neurons with no expression in muscle fibers.
source: Live fluorescent image (upper panel) and immunohistochemistry for GFP (lower panel) in a 4 dpf Tg(mnx1:gal4;UAS:GFP-aequorin-opt) zebrafish larva showing selective expression in spinal motor neurons (arrowhead: dorsal primary, arrow: ventral secondary motor neurons), and strictly no expression in muscle fibers (n = 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Acoustic stimulations triggered stereotypical escape responses characterized by an asymmetrical initial C-bend followed by fast swimming.
source: Acoustic stimulations triggered stereotypical escape responses characterized by an asymmetrical initial C-bend followed by fast swimming.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral observations and kinematic analysis.

claim: Acoustic stimulations led to stereotypical slow swims characterized by symmetrical bends with undulations propagating from rostral to caudal along the tail in 7.4% of trials.
source: In rare cases, possibly due to coelenterazine application, acoustic stimulations led to stereotypical slow swims characterized by symmetrical bends with undulations propagating from rostral to caudal along the tail (7.4% of trials, 21 out of 283 stimulations; see Mirat et al. [2013]) (Figure 1C–D, Videos 2–3, n = 10 larvae, see Budick and O'Malley, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the study.

claim: Stereotypical escape responses generated larger bioluminescence amplitudes than slow swims.
source: While time-to-peak and time decay of bioluminescence signals were invariant across maneuvers (data not shown), stereotypical escape responses generated larger bioluminescence amplitudes than slow swims (Figure 1D–E, mean bioluminescence amplitude = 30.8 + /- 1.4 photons/10 ms for escapes and 4.1 ± 1.6 photons/10 ms for slow swimming, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by bioluminescence measurements presented in the results.

claim: Bioluminescence signal amplitude correlated with the maximal angle of the tail bend.
source: Bioluminescence signal amplitude correlated with the maximal angle of the tail bend (Figure 1F, R = 0.4, p<0.001), suggesting that spinal motor neuron recruitment is increased during behaviors with larger tail bends and faster locomotor frequencies.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of bioluminescence and kinematic data.

claim: Spinal motor neuron recruitment is increased during behaviors with larger tail bends and faster locomotor frequencies.
source: Bioluminescence signal amplitude correlated with the maximal angle of the tail bend (Figure 1F, R = 0.4, p<0.001), suggesting that spinal motor neuron recruitment is increased during behaviors with larger tail bends and faster locomotor frequencies.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation between bioluminescence amplitude and tail bend angle.

claim: At 4 dpf, fictive locomotor burst frequencies ranged between 20–30 Hz for slow swims.
source: At 4 dpf, fictive locomotor burst frequencies ranged between 20–30 Hz for slow swims (left panel of Figure 2C, see Masino and Fetcho [2005]) and 20–80 Hz for escapes (right panel of Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ventral nerve root recordings shown in Figure 2C.

claim: At 4 dpf, fictive locomotor burst frequencies ranged between 20–80 Hz for escapes.
source: At 4 dpf, fictive locomotor burst frequencies ranged between 20–30 Hz for slow swims (left panel of Figure 2C, see Masino and Fetcho [2005]) and 20–80 Hz for escapes (right panel of Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ventral nerve root recordings shown in Figure 2C.

claim: During slow swimming, 23.2% of ventral motor neurons was active.
source: During slow swimming, a small fraction of ventral motor neurons was active (23.2%, left panel of Figure 2D, Figure 2E, Video 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: During escapes, 88.4% of motor neurons, including large dorsal motor neurons, was recruited.
source: In contrast, the majority of motor neurons, including large dorsal motor neurons, was recruited during escapes (88.4%, right panel of Figure 2D, Figure 2E, and Video 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: Dorsalmost motor neurons showed larger calcium transients than ventral ones.
source: Dorsalmost motor neurons showed larger calcium transients than ventral ones (Figure 2D), and the averaged ΔF/F across all recruited motor neurons was higher during escapes compared to slow swims (Figure 2F, mean ΔF/F/active cell = 91.1 + /- 4.7% during escape responses and 25.9 ± 3.8% during slow swimming, p<0.001, n = 10 larvae).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The averaged ΔF/F across all recruited motor neurons was higher during escapes compared to slow swims (91.1 ± 4.7% versus 25.9 ± 3.8%).
source: Dorsalmost motor neurons showed larger calcium transients than ventral ones (Figure 2D), and the averaged ΔF/F across all recruited motor neurons was higher during escapes compared to slow swims (Figure 2F, mean ΔF/F/active cell = 91.1 + /- 4.7% during escape responses and 25.9 ± 3.8% during slow swimming, p<0.001, n = 10 larvae).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The generation of fast escape responses requires the recruitment of more spinal motor neurons compared to slow swimming.
source: These data revealed that the generation of fast escape responses requires the recruitment of more spinal motor neurons compared to slow swimming and that the amplitude of calcium signals are higher in cells active during escapes compared to spontaneous swimming.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the calcium imaging data showing different recruitment patterns.

claim: The amplitude of calcium signals are higher in cells active during escapes compared to spontaneous swimming.
source: These data revealed that the generation of fast escape responses requires the recruitment of more spinal motor neurons compared to slow swimming and that the amplitude of calcium signals are higher in cells active during escapes compared to spontaneous swimming.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data comparing escapes and slow swimming.

claim: High bioluminescence signal amplitude during escape responses compared to slow swims results from the combination of a larger pool of active cells and larger calcium transients per active neuron.
source: Therefore, we conclude that high bioluminescence signal amplitude during escape responses compared to slow swims likely results from the combination of two effects: a larger pool of active cells driven by an increase in swimming frequency and larger calcium transients per active neuron.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined bioluminescence and calcium imaging data.

claim: Mean bioluminescence amplitude was markedly decreased in paralyzed compared to motile animals (26.6 ± 0.9 versus 11.1 ± 0.4 photons/10 ms).
source: Across all Tg(mnx1:gal4;UAS:GFP-aequorin-opt) larvae, mean bioluminescence amplitude was markedly decreased in paralyzed compared to motile animals (Figure 3B–C, signal amplitude before paralysis = 26.6 + /- 0.9 photons/10 ms; signal amplitude after paralysis = 11.1 + /- 0.4 photons/10 ms, p<0.001, n = 10 larvae).
evidence: This claim is supported by bioluminescence measurements before and after paralysis shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Within each larva, the mean normalized bioluminescence amplitude was decreased seven-fold after paralysis (0.056 ± 0.08 versus 0.36 ± 0.18).
source: Within each larva, the mean normalized bioluminescence amplitude was decreased seven-fold (0.056 ± 0.08 versus 0.36 ± 0.18, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by normalized bioluminescence measurements.

claim: Mean bioluminescence amplitude was markedly decreased in immotile cacnb1ts25/ts25 mutant larvae compared to motile control siblings (9.8 ± 0.4 versus 37.6 ± 1.4 photons/10 ms).
source: The mean bioluminescence amplitude was markedly decreased in immotile Tg(cacnb1ts25/ts25; mnx1:gal4; UAS:GFP-aequorin-opt) larvae compared to motile Tg(mnx1:gal4, UAS:GFP-aequorin-opt) control siblings (Figure 3D–E, mean signal amplitude in motile siblings = 37.6 + /- 1.4 photons/10 ms; mean signal amplitude in immotile mutants = 9.8 + /- 0.4 photons/10 ms, p<0.001, n = 3 larvae).
evidence: This claim is supported by bioluminescence measurements in mutant and control larvae shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: The recruitment of spinal motor neurons is enhanced during active locomotion.
source: Altogether these results demonstrate that the recruitment of spinal motor neurons is enhanced during active locomotion, indicating that mechanosensory feedback pathways recruited during muscle contraction contributes to increasing spinal motor output.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of bioluminescence in active versus paralyzed/immotile conditions.

claim: Mechanosensory feedback pathways recruited during muscle contraction contribute to increasing spinal motor output.
source: Altogether these results demonstrate that the recruitment of spinal motor neurons is enhanced during active locomotion, indicating that mechanosensory feedback pathways recruited during muscle contraction contributes to increasing spinal motor output.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results comparing active and fictive locomotion.

claim: The isl2b promoter drives expression in glutamatergic mechanosensory neurons, namely Rohon-Beard neurons and dorsal root ganglia in the spinal cord and trigeminal ganglia.
source: We expressed the zebrafish-optimized Botulinum toxin under the control of the isl2b promoter (Auer et al., 2015; Böhm et al., 2016; Sternberg et al., 2016) (see Materials and methods and Video 6) in order to block synaptic release in glutamatergic mechanosensory neurons, namely Rohon-Beard neurons (RB) and dorsal root ganglia (DRG) in the spinal cord and trigeminal ganglia (Figure 4A, note the bundle of RB and DRG axons ascending in the spinal cord in Figure 4B, (Won et al., 2011)).
evidence: This claim is supported by the expression pattern shown in Figure 4A-B and cited references.

claim: Tail-beat frequency was markedly reduced in BoTxBLC-GFP+ animals (34.2 ± 0.4 Hz versus 37.8 ± 0.3 Hz).
source: However, we noted that tail-beat frequency (TBF) (Figure 4E3) and, accordingly, speed (Figure 4E4) were markedly reduced in BoTxBLC-GFP+ animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by kinematic analysis data shown in Figure 4E3.

claim: Speed was markedly reduced in BoTxBLC-GFP+ animals (56.9 ± 1.1 versus 64.1 ± 0.9 mm/s).
source: However, we noted that tail-beat frequency (TBF) (Figure 4E3) and, accordingly, speed (Figure 4E4) were markedly reduced in BoTxBLC-GFP+ animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by kinematic analysis data shown in Figure 4E4.

claim: Escape duration increased in larvae deprived of mechanosensory feedback (from 168.1 ± 2.4 ms to 182.0 ± 3 ms).
source: Coincident with the reduction in TBF and stability of number of oscillations, the escape duration increased in larvae deprived of mechanosensory feedback (Figure 4E5, from 168.1 ± 2.4 ms to 182.0 ± 3 ms).
evidence: This claim is supported by kinematic analysis data shown in Figure 4E5.

claim: The amplitude of the first C-bend was not affected in BoTxBLC-GFP+ animals.
source: While the amplitude of the first C-bend was not affected in BoTxBLC-GFP+ animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), the amplitudes of subsequent tail bends were increased.
evidence: This claim is supported by kinematic analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The amplitudes of subsequent tail bends were increased in BoTxBLC-GFP+ animals, especially on the ipsilateral side.
source: While the amplitude of the first C-bend was not affected in BoTxBLC-GFP+ animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), the amplitudes of subsequent tail bends were increased. This was especially pronounced on the ipsilateral side, suggesting a modulation of motor circuits recruited after the response onset.
evidence: This claim is supported by kinematic analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Within the fast regime of the escape, silencing mechanosensory feedback reduces the distance travelled in BoTxBLC+ larvae compared to control siblings (5.9 ± 0.2 versus 7.4 ± 0.2 mm).
source: Within the fast regime of the escape, silencing mechanosensory feedback reduces the distance travelled in BoTxBLC+ larvae compared to control siblings (C1, 5.9 ± 0.2 versus 7.4 ± 0.2 mm, p<0.001), duration (C2, 60.0 ± 2.1 versus 67.8 ± 1.9 ms, p=0.005), number of oscillations (C3, 2.9 ± 0.1 versus 3.6 ± 0.1 oscillations, p<0.001), speed (C4, 104.3 ± 1.9 versus 112.6 ± 1.6 mm/s, p=0.001), and TBF (C5, 45.8 ± 0.4 versus 48.4 ± 0.3 Hz, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by kinematic analysis data shown in Figure 5C1.

claim: Within the fast regime of the escape, silencing mechanosensory feedback reduces duration in BoTxBLC+ larvae (60.0 ± 2.1 versus 67.8 ± 1.9 ms).
source: Within the fast regime of the escape, silencing mechanosensory feedback reduces the distance travelled in BoTxBLC+ larvae compared to control siblings (C1, 5.9 ± 0.2 versus 7.4 ± 0.2 mm, p<0.001), duration (C2, 60.0 ± 2.1 versus 67.8 ± 1.9 ms, p=0.005), number of oscillations (C3, 2.9 ± 0.1 versus 3.6 ± 0.1 oscillations, p<0.001), speed (C4, 104.3 ± 1.9 versus 112.6 ± 1.6 mm/s, p=0.001), and TBF (C5, 45.8 ± 0.4 versus 48.4 ± 0.3 Hz, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by kinematic analysis data shown in Figure 5C2.

claim: Within the fast regime of the escape, silencing mechanosensory feedback reduces number of oscillations in BoTxBLC+ larvae (2.9 ± 0.1 versus 3.6 ± 0.1 oscillations).
source: Within the fast regime of the escape, silencing mechanosensory feedback reduces the distance travelled in BoTxBLC+ larvae compared to control siblings (C1, 5.9 ± 0.2 versus 7.4 ± 0.2 mm, p<0.001), duration (C2, 60.0 ± 2.1 versus 67.8 ± 1.9 ms, p=0.005), number of oscillations (C3, 2.9 ± 0.1 versus 3.6 ± 0.1 oscillations, p<0.001), speed (C4, 104.3 ± 1.9 versus 112.6 ± 1.6 mm/s, p=0.001), and TBF (C5, 45.8 ± 0.4 versus 48.4 ± 0.3 Hz, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by kinematic analysis data shown in Figure 5C3.

claim: Within the fast regime of the escape, silencing mechanosensory feedback reduces speed in BoTxBLC+ larvae (104.3 ± 1.9 versus 112.6 ± 1.6 mm/s).
source: Within the fast regime of the escape, silencing mechanosensory feedback reduces the distance travelled in BoTxBLC+ larvae compared to control siblings (C1, 5.9 ± 0.2 versus 7.4 ± 0.2 mm, p<0.001), duration (C2, 60.0 ± 2.1 versus 67.8 ± 1.9 ms, p=0.005), number of oscillations (C3, 2.9 ± 0.1 versus 3.6 ± 0.1 oscillations, p<0.001), speed (C4, 104.3 ± 1.9 versus 112.6 ± 1.6 mm/s, p=0.001), and TBF (C5, 45.8 ± 0.4 versus 48.4 ± 0.3 Hz, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by kinematic analysis data shown in Figure 5C4.

claim: Within the fast regime of the escape, silencing mechanosensory feedback reduces TBF in BoTxBLC+ larvae (45.8 ± 0.4 versus 48.4 ± 0.3 Hz).
source: Within the fast regime of the escape, silencing mechanosensory feedback reduces the distance travelled in BoTxBLC+ larvae compared to control siblings (C1, 5.9 ± 0.2 versus 7.4 ± 0.2 mm, p<0.001), duration (C2, 60.0 ± 2.1 versus 67.8 ± 1.9 ms, p=0.005), number of oscillations (C3, 2.9 ± 0.1 versus 3.6 ± 0.1 oscillations, p<0.001), speed (C4, 104.3 ± 1.9 versus 112.6 ± 1.6 mm/s, p=0.001), and TBF (C5, 45.8 ± 0.4 versus 48.4 ± 0.3 Hz, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by kinematic analysis data shown in Figure 5C5.

claim: Within the slow component of the escape, silencing mechanosensory feedback in BoTxBLC+ larvae increases the distance travelled (3.5 ± 0.1 versus 2.4 ± 0.1 mm).
source: Within the slow component of the escape, silencing mechanosensory feedback in BoTxBLC+ larvae increases the distance travelled (D1, 3.5 ± 0.1 versus 2.4 ± 0.1 mm, p<0.001), duration (D2, 140.9 ± 3.4 versus 97.1 ± 3.2 ms, p<0.001, p<0.001) and number of oscillations (D3, 2.8 ± 0.1 versus 1.9 ± 0.1, p<0.001) but has no effect on speed (D4, 24.9 ± 0.4 versus 24.6 ± 0.4 mm/s, p=0.5) and tail-beat frequency (D5, 25.3 ± 0.1 versus 25.4 ± 0.1 Hz, p=0.5).
evidence: This claim is supported by kinematic analysis data shown in Figure 5D1.

claim: Within the slow component of the escape, silencing mechanosensory feedback in BoTxBLC+ larvae increases duration (140.9 ± 3.4 versus 97.1 ± 3.2 ms).
source: Within the slow component of the escape, silencing mechanosensory feedback in BoTxBLC+ larvae increases the distance travelled (D1, 3.5 ± 0.1 versus 2.4 ± 0.1 mm, p<0.001), duration (D2, 140.9 ± 3.4 versus 97.1 ± 3.2 ms, p<0.001, p<0.001) and number of oscillations (D3, 2.8 ± 0.1 versus 1.9 ± 0.1, p<0.001) but has no effect on speed (D4, 24.9 ± 0.4 versus 24.6 ± 0.4 mm/s, p=0.5) and tail-beat frequency (D5, 25.3 ± 0.1 versus 25.4 ± 0.1 Hz, p=0.5).
evidence: This claim is supported by kinematic analysis data shown in Figure 5D2.

claim: Within the slow component of the escape, silencing mechanosensory feedback in BoTxBLC+ larvae increases number of oscillations (2.8 ± 0.1 versus 1.9 ± 0.1).
source: Within the slow component of the escape, silencing mechanosensory feedback in BoTxBLC+ larvae increases the distance travelled (D1, 3.5 ± 0.1 versus 2.4 ± 0.1 mm, p<0.001), duration (D2, 140.9 ± 3.4 versus 97.1 ± 3.2 ms, p<0.001, p<0.001) and number of oscillations (D3, 2.8 ± 0.1 versus 1.9 ± 0.1, p<0.001) but has no effect on speed (D4, 24.9 ± 0.4 versus 24.6 ± 0.4 mm/s, p=0.5) and tail-beat frequency (D5, 25.3 ± 0.1 versus 25.4 ± 0.1 Hz, p=0.5).
evidence: This claim is supported by kinematic analysis data shown in Figure 5D3.

claim: Within the slow component of the escape, silencing mechanosensory feedback in BoTxBLC+ larvae has no effect on speed (24.9 ± 0.4 versus 24.6 ± 0.4 mm/s).
source: Within the slow component of the escape, silencing mechanosensory feedback in BoTxBLC+ larvae increases the distance travelled (D1, 3.5 ± 0.1 versus 2.4 ± 0.1 mm, p<0.001), duration (D2, 140.9 ± 3.4 versus 97.1 ± 3.2 ms, p<0.001, p<0.001) and number of oscillations (D3, 2.8 ± 0.1 versus 1.9 ± 0.1, p<0.001) but has no effect on speed (D4, 24.9 ± 0.4 versus 24.6 ± 0.4 mm/s, p=0.5) and tail-beat frequency (D5, 25.3 ± 0.1 versus 25.4 ± 0.1 Hz, p=0.5).
evidence: This claim is supported by kinematic analysis data shown in Figure 5D4.

claim: Within the slow component of the escape, silencing mechanosensory feedback in BoTxBLC+ larvae has no effect on tail-beat frequency (25.3 ± 0.1 versus 25.4 ± 0.1 Hz).
source: Within the slow component of the escape, silencing mechanosensory feedback in BoTxBLC+ larvae increases the distance travelled (D1, 3.5 ± 0.1 versus 2.4 ± 0.1 mm, p<0.001), duration (D2, 140.9 ± 3.4 versus 97.1 ± 3.2 ms, p<0.001, p<0.001) and number of oscillations (D3, 2.8 ± 0.1 versus 1.9 ± 0.1, p<0.001) but has no effect on speed (D4, 24.9 ± 0.4 versus 24.6 ± 0.4 mm/s, p=0.5) and tail-beat frequency (D5, 25.3 ± 0.1 versus 25.4 ± 0.1 Hz, p=0.5).
evidence: This claim is supported by kinematic analysis data shown in Figure 5D5.

claim: The reduction of speed and locomotor frequency observed in mechanosensory-deprived animals is specifically restricted to the fast component but not the slow one.
source: Therefore, the reduction of speed and locomotor frequency observed in mechanosensory-deprived animal is specifically restricted to the fast component but not the slow one (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential effects on fast versus slow components shown in Figure 5.

claim: Mechanosensory feedback enhances speed of locomotion by promoting the transition between fast and slow locomotion during escape responses.
source: Altogether, our results demonstrate that mechanosensory feedback enhances speed of locomotion by promoting the transition between fast and slow locomotion during escape responses.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the kinematic analysis showing effects on fast versus slow components.

claim: Spinal V2a interneurons are recruited in a topographic and frequency-dependent manner during fictive locomotion, with dorsalmost V2a interneurons solely active during fast locomotion.
source: Previous studies in zebrafish larvae showed that spinal V2a interneurons are recruited in a topographic and frequency-dependent manner during fictive locomotion, with dorsalmost V2a interneurons solely active during fast locomotion (McLean et al., 2008, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: V2a interneurons constitute an important class of excitatory interneurons driving the recruitment of motor neurons—especially during fast locomotion.
source: Ablation, silencing and optogenetic manipulations revealed that these neurons constitute an important class of excitatory interneurons driving the recruitment of motor neurons—especially during fast locomotion (Ampatzis et al., 2014; Bagnall and McLean, 2014; Crone et al., 2008; Kimura et al., 2006, 2013; Ljunggren et al., 2014; McLean et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Axonal projections from Rohon-Beard cells show patterns of perisomatic innervation of dorsal V2a cell bodies.
source: Interestingly, we noticed patterns of perisomatic innervation of dorsal V2a cell bodies by axonal projections originating from one cell type targeted by the isl2b driver, Rohon-Beard cells (Figure 6A–D, mean soma position of V2a = 0.72 + - 0.04, n = 12 cells in 4 larvae).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical observations shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: Rohon-Beard cells are low input resistance neurons and required current injections ranging from 200 to 700 pA to generate single spikes.
source: Rohon-Beard cells are low input resistance neurons and required current injections ranging from 200 to 700 pA to generate single spikes (Figure 7B, n = 6 cells, 250 ms injection steps).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Dorsalmost V2a neurons only required from 15 to 50 pA to fire action potentials.
source: In comparison, dorsalmost V2a neurons only required from 15 to 50 pA to fire action potentials (Figure 7H, n = 5 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 7H.

claim: 1 to 5 ms blue light pulses were sufficient to elicit photocurrents driving single action potentials in Rohon-Beard neurons at 4 and 5 dpf.
source: We found that 1 to 5 ms blue light pulses were sufficient to elicit photocurrents driving single action potentials in Rohon-Beard neurons at 4 and 5 dpf (Figure 7C and G, mean time to peak from the onset of the light pulse = 2.80 + /- 0.29 ms, n = 6 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic stimulation data shown in Figure 7C and G.

claim: RB stimulation led to short latency excitatory post-synaptic currents (EPSCs) in target V2a interneurons.
source: We found that RB stimulation led to short latency excitatory post-synaptic currents (EPSCs) in target V2a interneurons (Figure 7D–E and G, mean delay from the onset of light pulse = 3.71 + /- 0.19 ms, n = 8 cells in 8 larvae).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 7D-E and G.

claim: The lag between RB spikes time-to-peak and V2a EPSCs onset was below 1 ms (0.9 ms), a value compatible with monosynaptic connection.
source: To assess whether RB-V2A ipsilateral connection might be monosynaptic, we analyzed the lag between RB spikes time-to-peak and V2a EPSCs onset and found that it was below 1 ms (Figure 7G, 0.9 ms), a value compatible with monosynaptic connection (see Li et al. [2007a]) where cutoff is set at 3 ms for monosynaptic connections).
evidence: This claim is supported by timing analysis shown in Figure 7G and comparison to literature standards.

claim: Assuming a synaptic delay of 0.5 ms, the estimated conduction velocity along the axon of RB neuron would be 0.75 m/s.
source: Assuming a synaptic delay of 0.5 ms, the estimated conduction velocity along the axon of RB neuron would be 0.75 m/s, a value compatible with previous measurement in the field (Li et al., 2007a, 2004a).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the timing measurements and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: EPSC amplitude induced by RB stimulation in V2a interneurons were on average 28.14 ± 3.9 pA, leading to estimated depolarization of 11.71 ± 2.59 mV on target V2a.
source: EPSC amplitude induced by RB stimulation in V2a interneurons were on average 28.14 ± 3.9 pA, leading to estimated depolarization of 11.71 ± 2.59 mV on target V2a (n = 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements.

claim: In some cases, RB inputs were sufficient to elicit action potentials in V2a interneurons tested in current clamp mode.
source: In some cases, RB inputs were therefore sufficient to elicit action potentials in V2a interneurons tested in current clamp mode (Figure 7F).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Blockers of glutamatergic neurotransmission abolished EPSCs in target V2a.
source: Given the glutamatergic nature of RB neurons, we incubated the preparation with blockers of glutamatergic neurotransmission and found that it abolished EPSCs in target V2a (Figure 7I, n = 2 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 7I.

claim: There is a monosynaptic connection between RB neurons and ipsilateral dorsalmost V2a interneurons.
source: Altogether, these results indicate a monosynaptic connection between RB neurons and ipsilateral dorsalmost V2a interneurons and demonstrate the ability of RB neurons to recruit selectively a subpopulation of V2a interneurons controlling fast swimming in the dorsal spinal cord.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined optogenetic and electrophysiological data.

claim: RB neurons can recruit selectively a subpopulation of V2a interneurons controlling fast swimming in the dorsal spinal cord.
source: Altogether, these results indicate a monosynaptic connection between RB neurons and ipsilateral dorsalmost V2a interneurons and demonstrate the ability of RB neurons to recruit selectively a subpopulation of V2a interneurons controlling fast swimming in the dorsal spinal cord.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined anatomical, optogenetic, and electrophysiological data.

claim: The direct pathway from RB neurons onto ipsilateral 'fast' V2a neurons may act in concert with afferences from dorsal root ganglia and trigeminal neurons to enhance speed during active locomotion.
source: This direct pathway from RB neurons onto ipsilateral 'fast' V2a neurons may act in concert with afferences from dorsal root ganglia and trigeminal neurons to enhance speed during active locomotion.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: Mechanosensory feedback allows zebrafish larvae to travel the same distance in a shorter time (about 15 ms).
source: As it allows zebrafish larvae to travel the same distance in a shorter time (about 15 ms), mechanosensory feedback also bears ecological implications for fitness.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the kinematic data showing reduced escape duration with mechanosensory feedback.

claim: By speeding up escapes during a predator attack, mechanosensory feedback may help enhancing survival.
source: By speeding up escapes during a predator attack, mechanosensory feedback may help enhancing survival.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing an ecological implication based on the experimental findings.

claim: The amplitude of Aequorin signals from motor neurons could be used as a signature for distinguishing locomotor maneuvers including slow swimming and fast escape responses.
source: We found that the amplitude of Aequorin signals from motor neurons could be used as a signature for distinguishing locomotor maneuvers including slow swimming and fast escape responses that have specific ranges of swimming frequencies and distinct profiles of motor neurons recruitment (Liao and Fetcho, 2008; Masino and Fetcho, 2005; McLean et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by the bioluminescence data and cited literature on motor neuron recruitment.

claim: Eliminating mechanical sensory feedback originating from muscle contraction led to a decrease of bioluminescence signals from motor neurons during acoustic escape responses.
source: We found that eliminating mechanical sensory feedback originating from muscle contraction led to a decrease of bioluminescence signals from motor neurons during acoustic escape responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by the bioluminescence measurements in paralyzed versus active conditions.

claim: Mechanosensory feedback enhances the recruitment of motor circuits.
source: Our observations suggest that mechanosensory feedback enhances the recruitment of motor circuits.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the bioluminescence data comparing active and fictive locomotion.

claim: The perturbation of major kinematic parameters such as left/right coordination or locomotor frequency during fictive locomotion usually requires the ablation of entire classes of spinal neurons.
source: The perturbation of major kinematic parameters such as left/right coordination or locomotor frequency during fictive locomotion usually requires the ablation of entire classes of spinal neurons (Crone et al., 2008; Gosgnach et al., 2006; Talpalar et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There are no muscle spindles relaying mechanical information on muscle contraction to spinal circuits in fish.
source: Contrary to mammals, there are no muscle spindles relaying mechanical information on muscle contraction to spinal circuits in fish.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about fish anatomy.

claim: Glutamatergic stretch receptor neurons that can sense body elongation in lamprey project onto spinal sensory neurons, motor neurons and interneurons.
source: Instead, glutamatergic stretch receptor neurons that can sense body elongation in lamprey (Grillner et al., 1981; Rovainen, 1974) project onto spinal sensory neurons, motor neurons and interneurons (Di Prisco et al., 1990) and can entrain the locomotor central pattern generators (CPGs, [Grillner et al., 1981; McClellan and Sigvardt, 1988]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Stretch receptor neurons can entrain the locomotor central pattern generators in lamprey.
source: Instead, glutamatergic stretch receptor neurons that can sense body elongation in lamprey (Grillner et al., 1981; Rovainen, 1974) project onto spinal sensory neurons, motor neurons and interneurons (Di Prisco et al., 1990) and can entrain the locomotor central pattern generators (CPGs, [Grillner et al., 1981; McClellan and Sigvardt, 1988]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: GABAergic cerebrospinal-fluid contacting neurons have been shown to detect body curvature following muscle contraction in both zebrafish.
source: Recently, GABAergic cerebrospinal-fluid contacting neurons have been shown to detect body curvature following muscle contraction in both zebrafish (Böhm et al., 2016; Grillner et al., 1984; Jalalvand et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: The activation of mechanosensory pathways, either during natural mechanical oscillations of the tail or optogenetic stimulations, is sufficient to trigger locomotor activity.
source: Interestingly, the activation of each of these pathways, either during natural mechanical oscillations of the tail or optogenetic stimulations, is sufficient to trigger locomotor activity demonstrating that mechanosensory feedback can provide inputs to locomotor central pattern generator circuits in the spinal cord (Böhm et al., 2016; Fidelin et al., 2015; McClellan and Grillner, 1983; Wyart et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mechanosensory feedback can provide inputs to locomotor central pattern generator circuits in the spinal cord.
source: Interestingly, the activation of each of these pathways, either during natural mechanical oscillations of the tail or optogenetic stimulations, is sufficient to trigger locomotor activity demonstrating that mechanosensory feedback can provide inputs to locomotor central pattern generator circuits in the spinal cord (Böhm et al., 2016; Fidelin et al., 2015; McClellan and Grillner, 1983; Wyart et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cited studies showing activation of locomotion by mechanosensory pathways.

claim: A remarkably simple and conserved disynaptic cutaneous skin reflex relies on spinal mechanosensory neurons referred to as Rohon Beard (RB) neurons in Xenopus and zebrafish and 'dorsal cells' in lamprey.
source: Previous studies have described a remarkably simple and conserved disynaptic cutaneous skin reflex relying on spinal mechanosensory neurons referred to as Rohon Beard (RB) neurons in Xenopus and zebrafish and 'dorsal cells' in lamprey (Buchanan and Cohen, 1982; Christenson et al., 1988; Clarke et al., 1984; Easley-Neal et al., 2013; Li et al., 2003; Roberts et al., 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Spinal mechanosensory neurons respond to skin stimulation at rest by firing a single spike and project onto glutamatergic commissural interneurons.
source: In these species, spinal mechanosensory neurons respond to skin stimulation at rest by firing a single spike and project onto glutamatergic commissural interneurons (referred to as dIc, CoPA and giant interneurons respectively [Buchanan and Cohen, 1982; Easley-Neal et al., 2013; Li et al., 2003; Pietri et al., 2009; Sillar and Roberts, 1988]), which drive contralateral motor neuron activation and subsequent swimming away from the stimulus (Buchanan and Cohen, 1982; Christenson et al., 1988; Li et al., 2003, 2004b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Commissural interneurons drive contralateral motor neuron activation and subsequent swimming away from the stimulus.
source: In these species, spinal mechanosensory neurons respond to skin stimulation at rest by firing a single spike and project onto glutamatergic commissural interneurons (referred to as dIc, CoPA and giant interneurons respectively [Buchanan and Cohen, 1982; Easley-Neal et al., 2013; Li et al., 2003; Pietri et al., 2009; Sillar and Roberts, 1988]), which drive contralateral motor neuron activation and subsequent swimming away from the stimulus (Buchanan and Cohen, 1982; Christenson et al., 1988; Li et al., 2003, 2004b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: During swimming, excitation of commissural sensory interneurons from sensory neurons was shown to be filtered out by phase-locked inhibition.
source: During swimming, excitation of commissural sensory interneurons from sensory neurons was shown to be filtered out by phase-locked inhibition (Knogler and Drapeau, 2014; Sillar and Roberts, 1988), ensuring that the recruitment of RB neurons potentially arising from movement-related activation would not trigger the disynaptic cutaneous reflex.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Phase-locked inhibition ensures that the recruitment of RB neurons potentially arising from movement-related activation would not trigger the disynaptic cutaneous reflex.
source: During swimming, excitation of commissural sensory interneurons from sensory neurons was shown to be filtered out by phase-locked inhibition (Knogler and Drapeau, 2014; Sillar and Roberts, 1988), ensuring that the recruitment of RB neurons potentially arising from movement-related activation would not trigger the disynaptic cutaneous reflex.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cited studies on phase-locked inhibition.

claim: The contribution of RB neurons to the enhancement of speed by mechanosensory feedback is consistent with previous experiments showing that stimulation of RB neurons can reset or increase locomotor frequency in Xenopus tadpoles.
source: The contribution of RB neurons to the enhancement of speed by mechanosensory feedback is consistent with previous experiments showing that stimulation of RB neurons can reset or increase locomotor frequency in Xenopus tadoples (for example,[Sillar and Roberts, 1992]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The role of mechanosensory feedback to increase swimming speed is consistent with former observations in lamprey showing an entrainment of locomotion by mechanical stimulation of the spinal cord.
source: The role of mechanosensory feedback to increase swimming speed is consistent with former observations in lamprey showing an entrainment of locomotion by mechanical stimulation of the spinal cord (Grillner et al., 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: RB neurons have complex processes branching under the skin as well as ascending and descending in the spinal cord.
source: RB neurons have complex processes branching under the skin as well as ascending and descending in the spinal cord.
evidence: This claim is based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: RB neurons usually fire single action potentials.
source: Nonetheless measuring activation of RB neurons during mechanical stimulation remains challenging due to the fact that RB neurons usually fire single action potentials ( et al., 2017; Roberts et al., 2012; Winlove and Roberts, 2012) and most calcium indicator fail to report single spike without extensive averaging (see Chen et al. [2013]; Tian et al. [2009]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Most calcium indicators fail to report single spike without extensive averaging.
source: Nonetheless measuring activation of RB neurons during mechanical stimulation remains challenging due to the fact that RB neurons usually fire single action potentials ( et al., 2017; Roberts et al., 2012; Winlove and Roberts, 2012) and most calcium indicator fail to report single spike without extensive averaging (see Chen et al. [2013]; Tian et al. [2009]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Locomotion is faster in active compared to fictive conditions in various invertebrate as well as vertebrate species.
source: Altogether, our results about the role of mechanosensory feedback in speed modulation can explain the general observation made in various invertebrate as well as vertebrate species that locomotion is faster in active compared to fictive conditions.
evidence: This claim is based on general observations across species.

claim: In invertebrates, there is evidence in several species for fictive locomotor patterns being typically twice slower than real locomotion.
source: In invertebrates, there is evidence in several species for fictive locomotor patterns being typically twice slower than real locomotion (sea slugs, (Morton and Chiel, 1993), 1993; crayfish, (Bacqué-Cazenave et al., 2015); and fruit fly, (Mendes et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies in invertebrates.

claim: In the leech, the effect of denervation is a systematic slowdown of locomotor activity, although it is much larger in crawling (twofolds).
source: The leech is a particularly interesting example as it can perform both swimming and crawling. The effect of denervation is a systematic slowdown of locomotor activity, although it is much larger in crawling (twofolds) (Baader and Kristan, 1992; Eisenhart et al., 2000; Kristan and Calabrese, 1976).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies in leeches.

claim: In lamprey, the frequency of fictive swimming appears 5–10 times slower than the frequency of active swimming recorded through electromyography.
source: In lamprey where the same animal was used to compare active and fictive locomotion, the frequency of fictive swimming appears 5–10 times slower than the frequency of active swimming recorded through electromyography (Wallén and Williams, 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study in lamprey.

claim: The general slowdown of locomotor frequencies when peripheral sensory feedback is removed is commonly observed in fictive locomotion in mice.
source: The general slowdown of locomotor frequencies when peripheral sensory feedback is removed is commonly observed in fictive locomotion in mice as well (Bellardita and Kiehn, 2015; Talpalar et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies in mice.

claim: Microcircuit selection during locomotor behaviors is not only set by descending commands from supra-spinal centers but could rather result from a combination of inputs from descending and local spinal sensorimotor circuits recruited while the movement is performed.
source: Furthermore, our work demonstrates that microcircuit selection during locomotor behaviors is not only set by descending commands from supra-spinal centers but could rather result from a combination of inputs from descending and local spinal sensorimotor circuits recruited while the movement is performed.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental findings showing the role of mechanosensory feedback.

claim: The Tg(mnx1:gal4)icm11 line was based on the injection of the mnx1 construct provided by Dr. Thomas Auer and Dr. Filippo Del Bene.
source: The Tg(mnx1:gal4)icm11 line was based on the injection of the mnx1 construct provided by Dr. Thomas Auer and Dr. Filippo Del Bene (Institut Curie, Paris, France, see Table 1).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the generation of transgenic lines.

claim: The original sequence for GFP-Aequorin provided by Dr. Ludovic Tricoire was codon-optimized for expression in zebrafish.
source: The original sequence for GFP-Aequorin provided by Dr. Ludovic Tricoire (Université Pierre et Marie Curie, Paris, France) was subsequently codon-optimized for expression in zebrafish and subcloned into the PT2 14XUAS plasmid provided by Pr. Koichi Kawakami (National Institute of Genetics, Mishima, Japan).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the generation of transgenic lines.

claim: In homozygous cacnb1ts25/ts25 mutants, a mutation of the skeletal muscle dihydropyridine receptor β1a subunit interferes with the calcium release and mutant larvae are immotile.
source: In homozygous cacnb1ts25/ts25 mutants, a mutation of the skeletal muscle dihydropyridine receptor β1a subunit interferes with the calcium release and mutant larvae are immotile (Granato et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the original characterization of the mutant.
